value.overview: The Crested Owl (Lophostrix cristata) is a medium-sized, nocturnal forest owl named for its exceptionally long, whitish ear tufts. It is the only species in its genus and occurs from southern Mexico through Central America into northern South America. The species is elusive and most often detected by its deep, resonant calls rather than by sight. It generally depends on humid, mature tropical forest, although it may also use advanced secondary growth and wooded areas near streams.
value.classification: The Crested Owl belongs to the owl family Strigidae and order Strigiformes. Lophostrix is a monotypic genus, meaning that L. cristata is its only recognized species.
value.identification: Adults are dark brown to rich brown above, with a paler facial disk and underparts that may appear buff or whitish. The most distinctive feature is the pair of very long, pale ear tufts, which can give the head a horned appearance. The eyes are orange-brown to dark orange, the bill is mainly black, and the legs are yellowish. Juveniles are whitish and fluffy, with less contrasting facial markings and crest feathers.
value.rangeHabitat: The Crested Owl ranges from southern Mexico through Belize and Central America to northern South America, including the Amazon Basin in broad regions. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, occurring on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, especially in lowlands and foothills; it is generally uncommon but locally more frequent. Records extend from sea level to roughly 1,000–1,500 meters, with some occurrence near the Central Valley. It favors humid lowland and lower montane forest, river edges, forest clearings, dense understory, and mature secondary growth.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range; it is not known to undertake regular long-distance migration. Local movements may occur in response to food or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited, and the nest has not been well described. Available observations and reproductive data suggest breeding from the dry season into the beginning of the rainy season in parts of its range. Young may remain with or accompany their parents for some time after leaving the nest. The species is thought to use mature trees, snags, or natural cavities, but details of nest placement, clutch size, incubation, and parental care remain poorly documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Crested Owl appears to be an opportunistic nocturnal predator. Its diet includes large insects and other arthropods, as well as small mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians. It probably hunts from perches within forest interiors, edges, and clearings, dropping onto prey or making short flights to capture animals on vegetation or the ground. Detailed studies of its diet and hunting frequency are scarce.
value.behavior: This owl is strictly nocturnal, secretive, and difficult to observe during daylight. It commonly roosts alone or in pairs in dense vegetation, where its dark plumage provides concealment. At night it gives a deep, resonant call and may remain quiet for long periods. The long crest is conspicuous when raised but may be held less prominently while the bird is relaxed or roosting.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered decreasing, although the total population size and detailed population structure are poorly known.
